lede: Every layer of a leaf is shaped for a job: letting light through, catching it, letting gases move, keeping water in. Because a plant respires all the time and photosynthesises only in light, what goes in and out of a leaf depends on how bright it is.
can: Name each leaf layer and give its adaptation.
Explain the compensation point as equal rates and no net gas exchange.
Read hydrogencarbonate indicator and explain each tube in an experiment.

text: The leaf, gas exchange and the compensation point

md: A leaf is a flat solar panel a few cells thick. Light goes in at the top, gases move in and out through pores underneath, and sugar comes out. On a dull morning it can give out exactly as much carbon dioxide as it takes in.

alt: A cross-section through a leaf. From the top: a thin waxy cuticle, a single row of rectangular upper epidermis cells, a row of tall column-shaped palisade cells packed side by side and full of chloroplasts, a looser layer of rounded spongy cells with large air spaces between them and a few chloroplasts, then the lower epidermis, which is broken by a stoma between two curved guard cells.

prompt: The layer of the leaf where most gas exchange takes place is the ______ mesophyll.
explain: The spongy mesophyll — it is the one with air spaces. March 2026 examiners reported that few Foundation candidates could name it.

md:
Work down the leaf, and pair every structure with its **job**, because the job is what earns the mark.
**Waxy cuticle** — transparent so light gets through, waterproof so less water is lost, and a physical defence.
**Upper epidermis** — transparent for the same reason; its cell walls are a physical defence.
**Palisade mesophyll** — tightly packed, **end on** to the upper surface, with **many chloroplasts**, so it absorbs the most light and does most of the photosynthesis.

prompt: Why are palisade cells placed just under the upper surface, packed end on?
options: So the maximum amount of light reaches their many chloroplasts
So gases can diffuse between them
So water cannot escape from them
answer: So the maximum amount of light reaches their many chloroplasts
explain: Light first, and they have the chloroplasts to use it. Gas exchange is the spongy layer's job; waterproofing is the cuticle's.

md:
**Spongy mesophyll** — loosely arranged with **a few chloroplasts** and a **large surface area**; the **intercellular air spaces** between the cells let gases **diffuse** through the leaf.
**Guard cells and stomata** — the stomata are the pores, the guard cells open and close them, and gases **diffuse into and out of the leaf** through them. Most stomata are on the **lower** surface, out of the direct sun.

alt: Light micrograph of a stained leaf cross-section cut through the midrib: a single row of column-shaped palisade cells lies just under the upper surface on each side, rounded spongy cells with gaps between them fill the lower half, and a vascular bundle sits in the centre of the midrib
caption: A real leaf in section. The column-shaped palisade cells sit in a single row under the upper surface; the rounded spongy cells and their gaps fill the space below.
prompt: Name the layer where the cells are most tightly packed, and the layer with the largest air spaces. Which of the two would you expect to contain more chloroplasts, and why?

alt: Scanning electron micrograph of a single open stoma on a leaf surface, the pore framed by two sausage-shaped guard cells, with a ten micrometre scale bar printed along the bottom
credit: Charles Tschirhart, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
caption: One open stoma, seen down an electron microscope. The pore is framed by two guard cells; the scale bar is 10 micrometres.
prompt: Name the two cells either side of the pore, state which surface of the leaf most stomata are on, and use the scale bar to estimate the length of the pore.
Which structure lets gases move into and out of the leaf?
explain: The stomata, controlled by the guard cells. The cuticle is waterproof and the palisade layer is for light.

title: Two processes, running at the same time
md: A plant **respires all the time**, day and night, using oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. In the light it **also photosynthesises**, using carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen. What you measure from outside is only the **difference** between the two — the **net** exchange. That single idea explains every hydrogencarbonate indicator question CCEA has set.

prompt: A plant is in complete darkness. Which process is running?
explain: Respiration never stops; photosynthesis needs light.

alt: Three leaves. In the dark, arrows show carbon dioxide leaving and oxygen entering, labelled respiration only. At the compensation point an equals sign shows no net gas exchange. In bright light the arrows reverse: carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves.

caption: Same leaf, three light levels, three different net results.

md:
**In the dark** only respiration happens, so the leaf gives out carbon dioxide.
**In bright light** photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so overall the leaf takes carbon dioxide in.
**In between** there is a light intensity at which the **rate of photosynthesis exactly equals the rate of respiration**. That is the **compensation point**, and there is **no net gas exchange** at all.

alt: A graph of rate against increasing light intensity. A dashed horizontal line shows the rate of respiration staying roughly constant. A solid curve shows the rate of photosynthesis rising from zero. They cross at a marked point labelled compensation point; to the left of it respiration is faster, to the right photosynthesis is faster.

prompt: At the compensation point, the rate of photosynthesis is ______ to the rate of respiration.
explain: Equal. Say 'equal rates' and 'no net gas exchange' and you have both marks.

title: Why 'no net gas exchange' is not 'nothing is happening'
md: At the compensation point both processes are running hard. Every molecule of carbon dioxide made by respiration is used immediately by photosynthesis, and every molecule of oxygen made by photosynthesis is used by respiration. From outside, nothing crosses the leaf surface — but inside, both reactions are going at full speed. That word **net** is what an examiner is listening for.

prompt: At the compensation point, what would a gas sensor outside the leaf record?
explain: Both are running, but each uses what the other makes.

prompt: Hydrogencarbonate indicator has gone purple. What has happened to the carbon dioxide?
explain: Purple means less carbon dioxide, so photosynthesis has been faster than respiration.

title: Summer 2025 B1 Higher Q9(b) and Q9(c)(ii)
md: Asked for the colour after leaf discs had floated in bright light, most candidates correctly said **purple**. Asked for the colour after the same tube had been left in the dark, many said **yellow** — but examiners record 'many other colours seen, **including food test colours**'. Brick red, blue-black and lilac belong to §1.3 and mean nothing here. Three colours, one order: high yellow, normal red, low purple.

prompt: A leaf is sealed in a tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator and left in the dark for two hours. What colour does the indicator turn?
explain: In the dark only respiration happens, so carbon dioxide is added and the indicator goes yellow. Brick red is a Benedict's result and belongs to food tests.

md: **Tube A** has no leaf: it is the **control**, and it shows that any change in the others was caused by the leaf and not by the light or the temperature. **Tube B** is in the dark: respiration only, so yellow. **Tube D** is in bright light: photosynthesis wins, so purple. **Tube C** stays **red** — the leaf is at its **compensation point**, so there is no net gas exchange.

prompt: In tube C the indicator is still red after two hours. What does that show?
options: Photosynthesis and respiration are happening at equal rates
Neither photosynthesis nor respiration is happening
answer: Photosynthesis and respiration are happening at equal rates
explain: Red means no net change in carbon dioxide — the compensation point. Both processes are running; they simply cancel out.

title: Diffusion
attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder, licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://phet.colorado.edu)
task: Put a different number of particles on each side of the divider, remove it, and watch. Now say in one sentence why carbon dioxide moves into a brightly lit leaf through the stomata without the leaf doing anything to pull it in.

prompt: Why does carbon dioxide move into a brightly lit leaf through the stomata?
options: Photosynthesis keeps the concentration inside lower than outside, so it diffuses in
The guard cells pump it in
answer: Photosynthesis keeps the concentration inside lower than outside, so it diffuses in
explain: Diffusion down a concentration gradient. Photosynthesis uses the carbon dioxide as fast as it arrives, which keeps the gradient going.

A labelled diagram with layers to name and an adaptation to explain, and at Higher the last question of the paper: leaf discs, light intensity and indicator colours, with a trend, an explanation and a three-statement choice. Colour answers are one word, and the listing rule means two colours score nothing.
